content: The use of certain medications or therapies may lead to an increase in serum concentrations of thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, and cortisol-binding globulin. Consequently, the dosage of replacement thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy may need to be adjusted accordingly. In females with hereditary angioedema, the administration of exogenous estrogens can potentially trigger or worsen symptoms of angioedema. Chloasma, a condition characterized by hyperpigmentation of the skin, may develop during the use of certain medications, particularly in females with a history of chloasma gravidarum. Patients prone to developing chloasma should be advised to minimize exposure to sunlight or ultraviolet radiation while using the vaginal system. There have been reports of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) associated with the use of vaginal rings. TSS has also been linked to the use of tampons and certain barrier contraceptives. In some reported cases of TSS, vaginal ring users were concurrently using tampons. However, a definitive causal relationship between vaginal ring use and TSS has not been established. Notably, no cases of TSS were observed during clinical trials involving the vaginal system. If a patient presents with signs or symptoms suggestive of TSS, the vaginal system should be removed immediately, and appropriate medical evaluation and treatment should be initiated. Epidemiological studies and meta-analyses have not demonstrated an increased risk of genital or non-genital birth defects, including cardiac anomalies and limb-reduction defects, following exposure to combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) prior to conception or during early pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs, the vaginal system should be discontinued, as there is no clinical justification for the use of CHCs during pregnancy. Contraceptive hormones and/or their metabolites can be detected in human breast milk. CHCs may reduce milk production in breastfeeding females, with the likelihood of reduction being lower once breastfeeding is well established. Breastfeeding females should be advised to consider alternative methods of contraception until they have ceased breastfeeding. After using the vaginal system for 21 consecutive days, it should be removed and cleaned with mild soap and warm water. The device should then be dried with a clean cloth or paper towel and stored in its case during the one-week dose-free interval. At the end of this interval, the vaginal system should be cleaned again and reinserted for another 21-day cycle. For the most accurate and up-to-date information, contact the relevant plan provider.
